The money belt around his waist sagged and jiggled as he walked, and the empty rucksack which was slung over his shoulder flopped about in the breeze. It had been a good week for Yaakov Kerpil’s business— the merchandise had gone and money had come in. But Yaakov Kerpil had certainly worked hard for it, traveling tirelessly from village to village all week long. Only today, Friday, would he finally be able to return home

But before heading home, there were two stops he had to make. First, the rav’s house. Yaakov Kerpil stopped in front of a small but well-kept cottage on the main street in Tsharaye, right across from the shul.

The rav, Rav Shmuel Akiva, opened the door at Yaakov Kerpil’s first knock. He knew to expect him. The traveling businessman came to his house at the same time every week, like clockwork.

Shmuel Akiva coughed and cleared his throat. His beard and

hair were as white as snow, and his skin was a pasty white, almost translucent. It wasn’t because the rav was old, however; Yaakov Kerpil figured he couldn’t be that much older than himself. The rav’s body only looked aged due to his many years of fasting and sigufim.1

LAST TIME: Reb Kaddish and Freida arrange for Devorah Leah to meet Yosef Yitzchak. Before the meeting, Devorah Leah visits her parents’ kevarim to daven. During their meeting, she and Yosef Yitzchak talk about their families. Yosef Yitzchak starts telling a story about his father. The Pious

rav said, his eyebrows knitted together, and his eyes pinched and narrow. “Giving tzedaka brings great reward along with it, you know. Our Chachamim have said, ‘tzedaka tatzil mimaves—charity saves from death.’2 Our Chachamim also say, ‘miklal hein, ata shomei’a lav—from the positive [reward], one can understand the negative [punishment].’3

“Especially important is the tzedaka you give to the fund of talmidei chachamim. The most important mitzvah of all is Torah study—Talmud Torah k’neged kulam.’4 For those who cannot study themselves, giving money to support Torah scholars is the next best.”

From there, Yaakov Kerpil crossed the street for his second stop: the shul. He entered, looked right and left, and when he was sure no one was watching, he dropped a few more coins into the large tzedaka box. A couple of weeks back, in a fiery Shabbos drasha, the rav had spoken about the importance of giving tzedaka secretly. Yaakov Kerpil hadn’t understood much else from the speech, but those few sentences stuck out in his mind. Ever since then, he made sure to give some tzedaka this way, as well.

And now, after these two stops, Yaakov Kerpil was finally ready

to go home. When he arrived there, his wife, Tzippa Bracha, had a pail of cool water ready by the door and a bowl of hot chicken soup waiting at the table.

took another spoon of soup, then he sighed. “You know, today, when I gave the rav the money, he spoke about how the simple folk, like us, who don’t know how to learn Torah…” Yaakov Kerpil’s voice cracked

and he looked down into his bowl. “…can give money to those who learn in the beis midrash, and get a small part of the reward. And Tzippa Bracha, I couldn’t help but think … is this the most I can do? Shlep from town to town all week, and give just a little money at the end of it all? Is that really all I can do for Torah learning?”
